issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly defines moral incongruence as the interaction between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency, but later describes it as an interaction with severity of consequences. This changes the focal construct and creates ambiguity about what predictor will actually be tested. Because the hypotheses, power analysis, and interpretation depend on the definition of moral incongruence, this inconsistency undermines replicability and construct validity.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory participant eligibility for follow-up measures
issues.description: The manuscript alternately states that only past-year users will complete problematic-use measures and that problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants. These are different designs with different estimands, sample sizes, missing-data structures, and interpretability. Conditioning analyses on users versus including nonusers can substantially change interaction estimates involving frequency and disapproval.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory participant eligibility for follow-up measures
issues.description: This statement directly conflicts with the earlier statement that only past-year users will complete further problematic-use measures. The analysis plan depends on whether nonusers provide outcome data and whether nonuser responses are treated as zero, missing, or excluded.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.description: The analytic plan first states that the equivalence region will be based on a SESOI of δ = .27, then later states that the equivalence region is δ = |.11|. These are very different equivalence bounds and would lead to different conclusions about whether effects are practically null. This is a critical statistical inconsistency in the registered analysis plan.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.description: This later passage contradicts the previously stated δ = .27 and identifies δ = .11 as the equivalence region. The manuscript must specify one SESOI and justify it prospectively.
issues.quote: Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: Unstandardized interaction compared with standardized SESOI
issues.description: The plan says predictors will be entered in raw form and multiplied, but the equivalence region is based on standardized beta coefficients from prior studies. An unstandardized interaction coefficient from raw frequency and disapproval scales is not directly comparable to a standardized beta SESOI. For interactions, standardized coefficients require careful specification, typically standardizing constituent variables before forming the product or otherwise computing a standardized interaction effect. Without this, equivalence testing may use the wrong metric.
issues.quote: For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: Unstandardized interaction compared with standardized SESOI
issues.description: The equivalence criterion is explicitly defined using standardized estimates, but the model construction described elsewhere uses raw predictors. This mismatch makes the planned equivalence tests ambiguous and potentially invalid.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null

issues.subcategory: Equivalence power confused with detection power
issues.description: The power analysis is framed around detecting effects using conventional regression power, but the primary inferential goal for several hypotheses is equivalence testing. Power to detect a nonzero effect is not the same as power to conclude equivalence, which depends on confidence-interval precision relative to the equivalence bounds. The manuscript therefore does not establish adequate power for its planned equivalence conclusions.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015), a series of sensitivity analyses to determine the likely power our final sample sizes would have to detect the effect size associated with our SESOI and equivalence region defined above

issues.subcategory: Equivalence power confused with detection power
issues.description: The manuscript proposes altering analyses when sample sizes are underpowered for small effects, but justifies the alternative using power to detect a large effect rather than power to test equivalence. This does not support claims that smaller effects are null or practically null.
issues.quote: Even our smallest projected sample size (prescription drug misuse, at a prevalence of 3.5%, project n = 140) is more than sufficiently powered to detect such an effect (1 – β = .983).

issues.description: The manuscript variously refers to eight outcomes/moderations, seven target behaviors, and Table 1 implies nine behavior-by-outcome combinations if pornography and gambling are each analyzed with both validated scales and modified NIDA-ASSIST items. This ambiguity affects multiplicity, power, and the definition of primary versus secondary outcomes.
issues.quote: Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes.

issues.description: The analytic plan lists seven domains in the parenthetical but says there will be eight moderation analyses. Table 1 additionally lists both validated and modified ASSIST outcomes for pornography and gambling, implying more than eight possible outcome analyses.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use

issues.description: Frequency scales are described as 0–5 in some places and 1–6 in others. This affects centering, interpretation of intercepts, interaction terms, and comparability across domains. It also creates ambiguity about whether 'never' is coded as 0 or 1.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day).

issues.description: This later description conflicts with the 0–5 coding and with the supplemental materials, which use 0–5. The manuscript must specify a single coding scheme.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: Problem Gambling Severity Index scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods state that the PGSI uses a 0–3 scale, but the supplemental materials score response options as 0, 2, 4, and 5. This is not the standard PGSI scoring and would change scale totals, cutoffs, distributions, and regression coefficients. The discrepancy prevents replication and may invalidate comparisons with existing PGSI norms.
issues.quote: This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: Problem Gambling Severity Index scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The supplemental PGSI response coding conflicts with the methods section and with standard PGSI scoring.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.description: The methods state that BPS items are scored 0–2 and summed, but the supplemental materials score them 0, 2, and 4. This changes the scale range and may affect interpretation of severity and comparability with validation studies.
issues.quote: Participants will respond ... on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.description: The supplemental BPS response coding conflicts with the methods section and likely with the validated scoring of the BPS.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.description: The methods say gambling frequency will be assessed with a single item, but then say an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental materials show only one broad gambling frequency item. It is unclear whether there are multiple gambling behavior items or only one, which affects measurement reliability and the computation of the predictor.
issues.quote: We will assess gambling frequency using a single item.

issues.description: This sentence contradicts the single-item gambling frequency description and implies multiple gambling behavior indicators that are not shown.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.description: The manuscript describes the total N = 4,000 as including a nationally matched sample plus a large sports-wagering oversample. Unless appropriate weights, stratification, or separate analyses are used, the combined sample is not nationally representative and will overrepresent gambling involvement and correlates of gambling. This directly affects the central gambling comparisons and may also bias associations with substance use and pornography use.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore ... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: No survey weighting or design-based analysis plan
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify whether YouGov matching weights, post-stratification weights, oversample weights, or design-adjusted standard errors will be used. This is essential because the study makes population-level claims and includes a targeted sports-betting oversample. Unweighted OLS on the combined sample would not estimate U.S. population associations.
issues.quote: Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format. Accordingly, SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the study as nationally representative, but the base sample is matched only to age and gender norms and is supplemented by a sports-wagering oversample. Age-and-gender matching alone does not ensure representativeness on race, ethnicity, education, income, region, religiosity, political ideology, or internet/panel participation, all of which may relate to moral disapproval and addiction self-reports.
issues.quote: the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender

issues.description: The abstract presents the study as using a representative sample and an additional sports-wagering sample, but later implications refer to population-level effects. Without a clear weighting/stratification plan, the combined analytic sample cannot support population-generalized claims.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500).

issues.subcategory: Moral incongruence operationalized as interaction rather than discrepancy/distress
issues.description: The study equates moral incongruence with a statistical interaction between moral disapproval and frequency. However, moral incongruence conceptually refers to a perceived discrepancy between one's values and one's behavior, often accompanied by distress. A product interaction does not directly measure perceived discrepancy, conflict, distress, or the person's appraisal that their own behavior violates their values. This threatens construct validity of the focal predictor.
issues.quote: moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)

issues.subcategory: General moral disapproval does not measure self-directed incongruence
issues.description: The moral disapproval items ask whether the behavior is morally wrong in general, not whether the respondent sees their own behavior as violating their personal values, feels conflicted, or experiences distress. A person may think a behavior is generally wrong but not apply that judgment to their own context, or may personally regret behavior without endorsing a broad moral prohibition.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement “I believe that using ________ is morally wrong” on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.description: The focal moderator is measured with a single item for each behavior. Single items provide no internal consistency estimate, may have limited reliability, and cannot distinguish moral condemnation, health concerns, legal concerns, stigma, religious doctrine, or personal distress. Measurement error in the moderator and interaction term can attenuate effects and distort equivalence conclusions.
issues.quote: Moral disapproval of gambling will be assessed using a single item consistent with above-described items for substances and pornography use.

issues.subcategory: Criterion contamination by guilt/morality in pornography outcome
issues.description: The BPS includes an item about continuing pornography use despite guilt. Because guilt is closely tied to moral disapproval and moral incongruence, the outcome partly contains the construct used as the predictor. This criterion contamination can inflate associations between moral disapproval and problematic pornography use and makes it difficult to determine whether effects reflect addiction-like dysregulation or moral distress.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: Criterion contamination by guilt/morality in gambling outcome
issues.description: The PGSI includes an item asking about guilt over gambling. This overlaps conceptually with moral disapproval and moral incongruence. Associations between moral disapproval and PGSI scores may therefore reflect shared moral-affective content rather than gambling disorder symptoms per se.
issues.quote: Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?

issues.subcategory: Modified ASSIST outcome lacks validation for planned use
issues.description: The study substantially modifies the ASSIST/NIDA Quick Screen, adds pornography and gambling, changes response options, and averages items with different scoring ranges and timeframes. The resulting scores are not validated substance-use-disorder, gambling-disorder, or pornography-problem measures. This threatens validity of cross-domain comparisons and may alter psychometric properties.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Averaging items with incompatible scales and timeframes
issues.description: The modified ASSIST score averages three 0–5 past-three-month frequency items with two 0/3/6 lifetime/past-three-month items. Averaging these assumes equal intervals, equal weights, and comparable timeframes, none of which is justified. The resulting composite may be dominated by item scaling artifacts and may not represent a coherent severity construct.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to three frequency based questions ... on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) ... Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged

issues.description: The central claim concerns whether moral incongruence is unique to pornography versus other addictions, but the domains are assessed with different instruments, item content, scoring, timeframes, and degrees of moral contamination. Differences in interaction effects could reflect measurement differences rather than true domain specificity.
issues.quote: Alcohol | Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items for specific substances ... Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items ... Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items

issues.subcategory: Timeframe mismatch among predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Behavioral frequency is measured over the past 12 months, the BPS over the past 6 months, PGSI over the past 12 months, and modified ASSIST problem items over the past 3 months or ever. A cross-sectional interaction between past-year frequency and current/lifetime problems may not represent concurrent moral incongruence and can introduce temporal misclassification.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed ... past-year frequency of pornography use

issues.subcategory: Timeframe mismatch among predictors and outcomes
issues.description: The BPS outcome uses a 6-month window, whereas the pornography frequency predictor uses a 12-month window and the modified ASSIST items use mixed 3-month and lifetime windows.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, “In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?”

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency excludes partnered pornography use
issues.description: The pornography definition includes pornography generally, but the frequency item in the supplemental materials asks only about viewing pornography alone. This omits partnered pornography use and may misclassify frequency, especially for individuals whose pornography use occurs with partners. The predictor therefore may not align with the moral disapproval item or BPS outcome, which refer to pornography use more broadly.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: Frequency scale ignores dose, quantity, and exposure intensity
issues.description: The planned frequency predictor treats broad ordinal categories as the key behavioral severity indicator, but addiction risk depends heavily on dose, quantity, stakes, potency, route of administration, and duration. For alcohol, simply asking how often alcohol was consumed ignores number of drinks; for gambling, frequency ignores money wagered or losses; for nicotine, 'more than once per day' compresses large variation. This can bias interaction estimates and cross-domain comparisons.
issues.quote: for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: Ordinal frequency categories treated as interval predictors
issues.description: The frequency categories are ordinal and unevenly spaced: once/twice, monthly, weekly, daily, and more than once per day are not equal intervals. Treating them as continuous in OLS interaction models assumes equal spacing and linearity, which may not hold and can distort moderation effects.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Once or Twice (1) | Monthly (2) | Weekly (3) | Daily or Almost Daily (4) | More than Once Per Day (5)

issues.description: The categories 'illegal/illicit drugs' and 'prescription drugs for non-medical reasons' combine heterogeneous substances with different addictive potential, legal status, moral norms, patterns of use, and harms. A single frequency and moral-disapproval item for each broad category may not validly represent substance-specific moral incongruence or disorder symptoms.
issues.quote: Beginning with the NIDA Quick Screen, we will assess past year frequency of alcohol use, nicotine products, prescription drugs for non-medical reasons, and illegal drugs.

issues.description: For cannabis and illicit drugs, moral disapproval may reflect legal status, perceived criminality, regional law, or stigma rather than personal moral incongruence. The manuscript acknowledges heterogeneous cannabis laws but does not plan to measure or adjust for state legality, local availability, or criminalization.
issues.quote: given the heterogeneity of cannabis laws in the U.S. and the now-widespread, legal use of THC, we will add cannabis/THC related products to our focal substances, as it is commonly used but may no longer be considered illicit or illegal in many regions.

issues.description: The study is cross-sectional, but the manuscript uses causal terms such as 'influences,' 'contributor,' and 'affecting.' Cross-sectional associations cannot establish temporal ordering or causality; problematic use may increase moral disapproval, moral distress may increase perceived problems, or third variables may drive both.
issues.quote: we seek to establish whether moral incongruence ... influences self-perceived feelings of addiction

issues.description: This implication overstates what a cross-sectional survey can show. The study can estimate associations, not whether moral incongruence creates biased self-reports or false-positive diagnoses.
issues.quote: it would suggest that community and population-based research using self-reported symptoms of addiction might be systematically biased by participant morality

issues.description: The models adjust only for age, gender, and religiousness. Many plausible confounders may affect both moral disapproval and self-reported addiction symptoms, including political ideology, conservatism, mental health, shame proneness, impulsivity, sensation seeking, relationship status, socioeconomic status, education, race/ethnicity, region, legality, treatment history, and actual behavioral severity. Limited adjustment weakens causal or explanatory interpretations.
issues.quote: In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates

issues.description: People who experience consequences, failed control, stigma, or treatment contact may become more morally disapproving of the behavior after problems arise. The design does not establish whether moral disapproval precedes addiction self-reports or is a consequence of them.
issues.quote: we do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems

issues.description: All focal constructs are self-reported in the same survey, including sensitive behaviors, moral judgments, and addiction symptoms. Shared method variance, impression management, shame, and fear of disclosure may bias associations, especially for pornography and illicit substances. No validation, confidentiality details, or social-desirability adjustment is planned.
issues.quote: self-reported moral disapproval of various behaviors was related to self-perceived addiction to or problematic use of those behaviors

issues.description: The plan says that supplemental analyses will be conducted 'as appropriate' if assumptions are violated, but it does not specify which violations trigger which alternative models, what models will be used, or how discrepancies will be adjudicated. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom after seeing the data.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: OLS may be inappropriate for bounded ordinal/skewed outcomes
issues.description: The planned OLS regressions use summed or averaged ordinal symptom scales that are bounded, likely skewed, and potentially zero-inflated. Frequency predictors and moral-disapproval items are also ordinal. Although OLS can be robust in some settings, the primary plan does not prespecify ordinal, count, zero-inflated, or robust alternatives, making inference vulnerable to model misspecification.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software

issues.description: The manuscript proposes redefining the equivalence region using the observed pornography effect if gambling/substance effects exceed the original equivalence bounds. Although labeled exploratory, this data-dependent threshold can make conclusions about relative uniqueness contingent on observed results and may introduce circularity.
issues.quote: we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Alternative equivalence region changes the hypothesis
issues.description: For underpowered substance subgroups, the manuscript proposes replacing the null-equivalence test with a test against a much larger pornography-derived bound. This no longer tests whether the effect is practically null; it tests whether it is smaller than a prior pornography effect. The distinction is acknowledged but could still be conflated with support for the preregistered null-interaction hypotheses.
issues.quote: For these analyses, we would therefore not be able to evaluate equivalence with a null effect. However, by adjusting our equivalence region as indicated above, we would be able to infer whether the effect of moral incongruence was less than the effect observed in previous analyses focused on pornography use.

issues.subcategory: No multiplicity control for primary hypothesis tests
issues.description: The study plans numerous regressions across substances, gambling, pornography, direct effects, interactions, equivalence tests, and possibly multiple outcomes for pornography and gambling. Only bivariate correlations are described as Holm-adjusted; there is no stated familywise or false-discovery plan for the primary regression tests. This increases the chance of false-positive conclusions and selective emphasis.
issues.quote: Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

issues.subcategory: No clear preregistration or registered-report repository details
issues.description: Although the manuscript is labeled a Registered Report, it does not provide a registry link, version, date, embargo status, analysis code, or clear distinction among confirmatory, secondary, and exploratory analyses. This limits transparency and makes it harder to evaluate deviations after data collection.
issues.quote: Moral Incongruence and Addiction: A Registered Report

issues.subcategory: Data collection may be embedded in larger study without firewall details
issues.description: The study is derived from a larger funded project. The manuscript does not specify whether the focal data will be collected only after Stage 1 acceptance, whether investigators will be blinded to relevant variables before finalizing the plan, or how other measures/analyses from the larger project could influence decisions. This creates potential analytic flexibility despite the registered-report format.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming.

issues.description: The manuscript relies on YouGov's proprietary procedures but does not report recruitment sources, eligibility, response rates, completion rates, incentives, matching variables beyond age and gender, weighting procedures, exclusion rules, or panel quality metrics. These details are necessary to evaluate selection bias and replicability.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.description: The manuscript states that no exclusions are anticipated because YouGov guarantees quality control, but it does not specify attention checks, speeding checks, duplicate detection, straightlining criteria, bot detection, or how failed quality checks will be handled. Reliance on proprietary standards limits reproducibility and may leave careless responding unaddressed.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding.

issues.description: The manuscript assumes there will be no unplanned missingness, but sensitive survey items often produce skipped responses, refusals, 'prefer not to answer' responses, or panel covariate missingness. The analysis plan does not specify listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, imputation, treatment of structural missingness, or handling of incomplete surveys.
issues.quote: Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: No dropout or incomplete-survey reporting plan
issues.description: The manuscript does not state how many invited participants are expected, how many may begin but not complete the survey, or how partial completions will be treated. This is particularly relevant for sensitive topics such as pornography, gambling, and illicit drug use, where item nonresponse or dropout may be systematic.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that prescription drug misuse and illicit drug use subgroups may be too small to detect the SESOI or test equivalence. These underpowered subgroups are central to the claim that moral incongruence does not generalize to substance use disorders, so inconclusive estimates could be misinterpreted as evidence of absence.
issues.quote: in the case of illicit drug use ... and prescription drug misuse ... it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.description: The planned covariate coding collapses everyone who is not male into a single 'not-male' category, potentially combining women, nonbinary respondents, and missing/other responses. This may obscure gender differences and creates ambiguity for gender-specific alcohol screening items that are only defined for man/woman categories.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.description: The supplemental materials say the male alcohol item asks about more than 5 drinks, but the response-row label says 'More than four drinks.' This creates ambiguity in the actual questionnaire and may affect heavy-drinking measurement.
issues.quote: IF GENDER = MAN In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)

issues.description: The theoretical motivation concerns CSBD, but the primary sexual-behavior outcome is problematic pornography use or self-perceived pornography addiction. CSBD is a clinical diagnosis requiring broader assessment of dysregulation, impairment, exclusions, and differential diagnosis. Findings on pornography self-report scales cannot directly validate or invalidate ICD-11 CSBD diagnostic caveats.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model for understanding self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography. Furthermore, should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.

issues.subcategory: Diagnostic-caveat inference does not follow from interaction test
issues.description: The ICD-11 caveat concerns whether distress based solely on moral judgments is sufficient for diagnosis. The proposed statistical interaction between frequency and moral disapproval does not directly test whether moral distress alone causes false-positive CSBD diagnoses or whether clinicians should include an exclusion. The inference from moderation to diagnostic validity is conceptually too strong.
issues.quote: Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.description: The manuscript frames CSBD as uniquely containing a moral-distress caveat across all diagnostic manuals. Even if CSBD has a specific caveat, many diagnostic systems include cultural, religious, normative, impairment, and bereavement/exclusion considerations across diagnoses. The broad claim risks overstating the theoretical distinctiveness of CSBD and the implications of the proposed study.
issues.quote: At present, CSBD is the only recognized disorder in any diagnostic manual to include such a caveat

issues.subcategory: Confirmatory aim phrased as demonstrating favored hypothesis
issues.description: The stated goal is to demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior, rather than neutrally testing whether it is unique. This framing may bias interpretation of ambiguous or mixed findings and is inconsistent with the evidentiary neutrality expected in confirmatory registered reports.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Self-perceived addiction conflated with validated symptom scales
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly describes the dependent variable as self-reported feelings of addiction, but some outcomes are symptom indices or screeners, not direct measures of perceived addiction. Conversely, modified ASSIST and PGSI items capture consequences and failed control rather than subjective addiction identity. This construct slippage complicates interpretation.
issues.quote: key dependent variables are listed in Table 1

issues.description: The manuscript draws implications about false-positive diagnoses and clinical assessment, but the study uses community self-report screeners without clinician interviews, impairment verification, differential diagnosis, or assessment of whether symptoms are attributable solely to moral distress. It therefore cannot estimate false-positive diagnosis rates.
issues.quote: the real potential concern associated with this effect is whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings.

issues.subcategory: No control for actual behavioral severity beyond frequency
issues.description: The key interaction uses frequency as the behavior component, but addiction severity depends on many behavioral features beyond frequency. Without controlling for quantity, duration, intensity, money spent, consequences, tolerance, withdrawal, or attempts to quit, moral-disapproval effects may be confounded with unmeasured severity differences among users.
issues.quote: moral disapproval of the behavior in question ... will be tested as a moderator in the relationship between the frequency of engaging in a behavior and self-reported problems with or addiction to that behavior.

issues.subcategory: Unclear handling of covariates from panel data
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are taken from YouGov panel data rather than measured in the survey, but the manuscript does not report when these data were collected, whether they will be updated, how missing or inconsistent panel data will be handled, or how categorical gender will be coded before binary conversion.
issues.quote: Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey).

issues.description: Religiousness will be computed by standardizing Pew items and averaging them. If standardization is done within the combined sample that includes the sports-betting oversample, the covariate's metric becomes sample-dependent and may not correspond to the U.S. population distribution. This affects replicability and interpretation of coefficients.
issues.quote: Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items taken from Pew Research Center

issues.subcategory: No exact model formula or coding details
issues.description: The analytic plan does not fully specify model equations, whether covariates are included in equivalence tests, how categorical variables are coded beyond gender, whether weights are included, whether predictors are standardized before interaction construction, and whether analyses are one- or two-sided. These omissions limit reproducibility.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests using the reg.equiv.fd function

issues.subcategory: Moral-disapproval items not behavior-specific enough for gambling
issues.description: The gambling moral-disapproval item refers to gambling globally, but the frequency item combines lotteries, casino gambling, fantasy sports, esports betting, sports betting, cards, and online betting. Moral beliefs may differ substantially across these activities, so a global moral-disapproval item may not match the specific behavior driving frequency or problems.
issues.quote: Examples of these types of activities include: gambling in casinos or online, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money, placing bets on esports, placing bets on traditional sporting events, playing cards for money, placing bets online.

issues.subcategory: Moral-disapproval items not behavior-specific enough for nicotine
issues.description: The nicotine category combines cigarettes, smoked tobacco, smokeless tobacco, e-cigarettes, and vaping. Moral evaluations and addiction profiles may differ across these products. A single moral-disapproval and frequency item may obscure product-specific relationships.
issues.quote: smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.

issues.subcategory: Direct comparison of uniqueness not primary-tested
issues.description: The hypotheses infer uniqueness from whether interactions are significant/equivalent within separate domain-specific regressions. However, differences in significance across models do not establish that coefficients differ between domains. A direct comparative model or formal test of interaction-effect heterogeneity is needed to support claims of uniqueness.
issues.quote: should we find that moral incongruence ... only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model

issues.description: The study is a U.S. online-panel, cross-sectional community survey, but the manuscript discusses implications for clinical diagnosis and treatment-seeking populations. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but several earlier claims still imply diagnostic and clinical relevance that the design cannot directly support.
issues.quote: there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD

issues.subcategory: Funding source not integrated into conflict-of-interest discussion
issues.description: The study is funded by a gambling-related organization and includes a large sports-wagering oversample, but the manuscript does not provide a conflict-of-interest statement, funder role, data access independence, or safeguards against sponsor influence. This is important for evaluating potential bias in gambling-related research.
issues.quote: funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming

issues.description: The manuscript sometimes treats tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine as separate outcomes and elsewhere combines them into one tobacco/nicotine item. This affects the number of target behaviors, power analysis, and interpretation of nicotine-related findings.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.description: This statement indicates a single combined tobacco/nicotine question, conflicting with the later parenthetical that implies tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine are separate substances.
issues.quote: we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.
